newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Grains and coffee strong, lumber and oil also rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Grains and coffee strong, lumber and oil also rise.

text.p: Grain and soybean prices rose on Thursday amid strong exports and a final blast of wintry weather in the Midwest that prompted worries about crop damage, planting delays and flooding.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for May delivery rose 4-3/4 cents a bushel to close at $3.03-3/4. May delivery wheat closed up 7-1/2 cents at $3.93 and May soybeans up 7-3/4 cents at $8.55-1/4.
Meteorologists said frigid temperatures that are expected to persist through the weekend could damage winter wheat from Kansas to Texas that is just emerging from dormancy at the start of spring.
"We are talking about the likelihood of some damaging cold temperatures for southern Plains wheat this weekend," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist for Weather Services Corp.
Meanwhile, in the Red River Valley of North Dakota, college students on Thursday joined sandbagging efforts ahead of the river's expected record crest.
The area, the heart of the spring wheat belt, may see acreage losses as well as stiff planting delays that could hurt yields.

Corn and soybean prices rose on stronger than expected weekly export sales reported by the Agriculture Department, which underscored that neither record South American crops or the strong dollar were slowing demand for American grain.

Net exports of corn during the week ended April 3 totaled 929,500 metric tons, well above analysts' predictions of sales of 400,000 to 600,000 tons. Soybean sales of 308,500 tons compared to expectations for 150,000 to 250,000 tons.
"The numbers again tell us we're not curtailing usage at these price levels," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
Rice futures also rose as exports of 41,000 tons surpassed expectations of 18,000 to 28,000 tons. Rice for May delivery closed up 9 cents at $11.36-1/2 per hundred pounds.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber prices soared for a third straight day. Lumber for May delivery closed up $9.90 at $411.50 per thousand board feet.

Traders said cash lumber demand had suddenly boomed this week after fears were dispelled that Canadian wood shipments would pick up dramatically after April 1, the start of a new 12-month period of voluntary quota supplies.
That has not been the case, so many lumber yards have been left short of wood heading into the spring and summer season when construction picks up.
"Cash is very strong. Wood is very tight," said Roger Champagne, marketing manager for Capital Forest Products Inc.
"A lot of people were under the assumption that there was going to be this wall of wood to come down from Canada after the first because of the quota, but it's just not there."
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices finished mostly higher as traders still worried about supplies this year.
Coffee for May delivery closed at 191.05 cents a pound, up 1.35 cents.

A strike by truckers in Colombia, the number two coffee exporter, was scheduled for April 20. Elsewhere, the National Coffee Council in leading exporter Brazil said coffee stocks held by Brazilian cooperatives on March 31 totaled 1.49 million bags, down from 2.07 million a month earlier.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil prices rose sharply as unseasonably cold weather descended on the northeastern United States. The surprising return of wintry weather also boosted crude oil and gasoline.

"It's pretty chilly here for this time of year, and it is supposed to continue," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products with Paribas Futures in New York. "This caught people by surprise, so there was a lot of short covering."

Heating oil for May delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange ended up 1.75 cents a gallon at 54.86 cents. May crude oil closed up 30 cents at $19.57 a barrel and May gasoline up 0.37 cent a gallon at 61.07 cents.
The National Weather Service said it expects temperatures to remain below normal in the Northeast through next week, extending the chilly start of spring.
